column2: Among such degraded, outcaste, evil-minded Bahlikas, what sensible man would live even for a moment?
Such are the Bahlikas of futile conduct, as a Brahmana described; of both their good and evil deeds you take a sixth share.
Having said this, the good Brahmana further spoke a reply; hear what was said of the undisciplined Bahlikas.
There a rakshasi sings always on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, beating a drum at night in the prosperous city of Shakala:

When will the town-criers again sing songs in Shakala, satisfied with beef and meat, having drunk the great Gauda liquor,
mahabharata:8:30.31	adorned, with tall fair women, eating onions, gandusha and many sheep?
mahabharata:8:30.32	Those who do not eat pork, fowl, beef, ass, camel and sheep meat—their birth is in vain.
Thus sing the drunken people of Shakala with liquor, with children and old people leaping; how could there be good conduct among them?
Know this, Shalya; and I tell you more of what another Brahmana said of us in the Kuru assembly.
Where these five rivers flow, and the pilu forests too—the Shatadru, Vipasha, third the Iravati, the Chandrabhaga and the Vitasta, with the Sindhu as sixth—those outside them,
those countries called Aratta, of lost dharma, are not to be visited, of the outcaste, the Dashamiyas, the Videhas, the non-sacrificers.
Gods, fathers and Brahmanas do not accept anything from those Bahlikas whose dharma is lost; so the tradition says.
A learned Brahmana rightly said in the assembly that the Bahlikas, merciless, eat in wooden and earthen bowls smeared with barley, licked by dogs and the like.
The Bahlikas eat and drink sheep's, camel's and ass's milk and its products.
Confusers of offspring, wretches, eaters of everything but milk, the Bahlikas called Arattas are to be avoided by the wise.
Know also, Shalya; and I tell you more of what another member of the assembly, a Brahmana, said in the Kuru assembly.
Having drunk milk at Yugandhara and lived at Achyutasthala, and likewise bathed at Bhutilaya, how will he go to heaven?
Where these five rivers flow forth from the mountain, the Arattas called Bahlikas—an Aryan should not dwell among them even two days.
Bahis and Halika are two pishachas on the Vipasha; the Bahlikas are their offspring, not a creation of the Lord of Creatures.
One should avoid Kara, Karaka, Mahishaka, the Kalingas, the Kikata forest, Karkotaka, Viraka and the wicked ones.
Thus a rakshasi, living for one night in a shami-wood house with a great mortar for girdle, said to a pilgrim:
Those countries are called Aratta, those people Bahlikas; the Sindhu and Sauviras dwell there, mostly despised.
Know also, Shalya; and I tell you more; hear what I say with attention.
A Brahmana, once a guest, went to the house of an artisan, and seeing his conduct there, pleased, said to the artisan:

I have long lived on a single peak of the Himalaya and seen many countries filled with various dharmas.
mahabharata:8:30.51	These peoples are not at odds in any dharma, for all of them taught dharma as stated by the masters of the Veda.
mahabharata:8:30.52	But wandering always among countries full of various dharmas, I observed among the Bahlikas, O great king:
mahabharata:8:30.53	There a man having been a Brahmana becomes a kshatriya, then a vaishya and a shudra, and then a Bahlika becomes a barber.
mahabharata:8:30.54	Having become a barber, he again becomes a Brahmana, and having become twice-born there, he is again born a slave.
mahabharata:8:30.55	In one family there is one Brahmana, and the others act at will; the Gandharas, Madrakas and some Bahlikas are senseless.
mahabharata:8:30.56	This I heard there, a cause of confusion of dharma; having wandered the whole earth, I found reversal among the Bahlikas.
Know also, Shalya; and I tell you more of what another said in disparagement of the Bahlikas.
Long ago a chaste Aratta woman was carried off by robbers, and when she was approached unrighteously, she cursed them:
Since you approach me, a young girl with kinsmen, unrighteously, therefore the women in your families will be unchaste, and you lowest of men will not be freed from this dreadful sin.
The Kurus with the Panchalas, Shalvas, Matsyas and Naimishas, Kosalas, Kashis, Angas, Kalingas and Magadhas,
and the Chedis, of great fortune, know eternal dharma; and good people in many countries are mostly of that kind (the line is obscure in this text).
From the Matsyas up, the Kuru-Panchala people, and the distinguished Chedis, up to Naimisha, the good live by ancient dharma—except the Madras and the crooked five-river people.
Knowing so, O king, of the tales of dharma, Shalya, you stay silent like a dullard. You are that people's protector and king, taker of a sixth of their good and bad deeds.
Or rather you are the taker of their evil, not protecting them; the king who protects partakes of merit, you of the demerit.
When dharma was formerly honoured in all countries, eternal, seeing the dharma of the five rivers the Grandsire said "Fie!"
Even in the Krita age, of the outcast Dashamiyas of inauspicious deeds, the Grandsire despised the dharma of the five rivers; he would not honour it among varnas established in their own dharma.
Know also, Shalya; and I tell you more: Kalmashapada, sinking in a lake, a rakshasa, said:
Begging is the stain of a kshatriya, untruth the stain of a Brahmana, the Bahlikas the stain of the earth, the Madra women the stain of women.
A king, raising the sinking night-ranger, asked him, and he explained, saying what you should hear.

The stain of men is the Mlecchas, the stain of Mlecchas the Maushtikas, of Maushtikas the eunuchs, of eunuchs the priests of kings;
mahabharata:8:30.71	and whatever is the stain of those for whom royal priests sacrifice, and of the Madrakas, that would be your stain if you do not release us.
So it is said that this was an effective remedy against rakshasa-afflicted and poison-struck, a spoken reply once accomplished.

Brahman among the Panchalas, own-dharma among the Kauravas, truth among the Matsyas and Shurasenas, sacrifice among the easterners, serfs among the southerners, thieves among the Bahlikas, mixture among the Surashtras.
Ingratitude, seizing others' property, drinking liquor, and approaching a teacher's wife—for those whose dharma it is, there is no unrighteousness; fie on the Arattakas and five-river people.
From the Panchalas up, the Kurus, Naimishas and Matsyas know dharma; the Kalingas, Angas and Magadhas, the elders, live by the remaining dharmas.
The eastern quarter is resorted to by the gods led by Agni; the southern is guarded by the fathers and Yama of good deeds.
The western is protected by Varuna, guarding the asuras, the mighty; the northern by the Lord Soma, devoted to Brahmanas, with Brahmanas.
Himavat guards rakshasas and pishachas, Gandhamadana the guhyakas; Dhruva all beings; Vishnu, Janardana, the worlds.
The Magadhas understand hints, the Kosalas what is seen, the Kuru-Panchalas half-spoken words, the Shalvas full commands; the mountaineers are rough like their mountains.
The Yavanas, O king, know everything and are especially brave; Mlecchas are regulated by their own signs; no other people speak unprompted.
But the Bahlikas are stubborn, and none of the Madrakas are otherwise. Such as you, Shalya, ought not to answer.
Knowing this, be silent and do not oppose me; I will first slay you and then slay Keshava and Arjuna."
[Shalya said:] "The abandonment of the afflicted and the sale of one's wife and sons occur among the Angas, of whom you are the lord.
Knowing the faults in yourself, which Bhishma stated when you were counted among chariot-warriors and maharathas, be free of anger and do not be wrathful.
Brahmanas exist everywhere, kshatriyas exist everywhere, vaishyas and shudras too, Karna, and chaste women of good vows.
Men delight in jesting with men, ridiculing one another, country by country, in union with their wives.
Everyone is always skilled in speaking of others' faults; he does not know what is to be said of himself, or, knowing, is bewildered."
[Sanjaya said:] Karna made no reply, and Shalya too faced the enemy; Radheya, laughing again, urged him: "Go on."
He went forth with the roar of the chariot, lion-roars and the sounds of instruments, as if making the earth tremble.
Trembling as if with rage, keen for battle, the scorcher of foes of great splendour, O best of the Bharatas, arranged his array duly.
Like Maghavan the asura host, he destroyed the Pandava army and, overpowering Yudhishthira, he made him go to the left.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "How, Sanjaya, did Radheya counter-array against the Pandavas, the heroes led by Dhrishtadyumna and protected by Bhimasena?
And what were the flanks and wings of my army, Sanjaya; how were they divided duly and how stationed?
And how did the sons of Pandu counter-array against my men, and how did this dreadful great battle begin?
Where was Bibhatsu when Karna went to Yudhishthira? For who could approach Yudhishthira in Arjuna's presence?
He who alone conquered all beings at Khandava long ago—who but Radheya, wishing to live, would fight him elsewhere?"
[Sanjaya said:] Hear the arrangement of the array, how Arjuna came, having entrusted the king to them, and how the battle took place.
Kripa Sharadvata, O king, the valiant Magadha and Kritavarman the Satvata took up the right wing.
On their flank Shakuni and the great chariot-warrior Uluka guarded your army with horsemen bearing bright lances.
With the unflustered Gandharas and the unconquerable mountaineers, like swarms of locusts, like fearsome pishachas,
thirty-four thousand chariots that never retreat—the Samshaptakas, keen for battle—guarded the left side.
Gathered by your sons, wishing to kill Krishna and Arjuna, their flank was the Kambojas and Shakas with the Yavanas.
At the order of the charioteer's son, with chariots, horses and foot-soldiers, they stood challenging Arjuna and mighty Keshava.
In the middle, at the front of the army, Karna stood armoured, wearing bright armour and armlets and a garland, protecting the front of the host.
Guarded by his enraged sons, the best of weapon-bearers, the hero shone, leading the head of the army.
Duhshasana, with iron-hard arms, mighty-armed, blazing like sun and fire, tawny, pleasing to see, mounted on the shoulders of a great elephant, surrounded by troops, stood at the rear of the array.
Behind him, O great king, came King Duryodhana himself, guarded by his brothers with variegated horses and variegated armour.
Guarded by the valiant Madras and Kekayas together, he shone, O great king, like Shatakratu with the gods.
Ashvatthaman and the heroic great chariot-warriors of the Kurus, with ever-rutting elephants ridden by brave Mlecchas, followed that chariot division, dripping like clouds.
With banners, pennants and blazing excellent weapons, mounted by horsemen, they shone like trees on mountains.
Thousands of foot-guards for those infantry and elephants, brave swordsmen and pattisha-bearers, never retreated.
With horsemen, chariots and elephants, more richly adorned, that king of arrays shone like the host of gods and asuras.
The Brihaspati array, well arranged by the wise leader, seemed to dance, putting fear in the enemy.
From its flanks and counter-flanks warriors eager to fight poured out, infantry, horse, chariots and elephants, like clouds in the rains.
Then, seeing Karna at the head of the army, King Yudhishthira spoke to Dhananjaya, slayer of foes, the sole hero:

See, Arjuna, the great array made by Karna in battle; with its flanks and counter-flanks the army shines.
mahabharata:8:31.30	Having seen this great force of the enemy, let such a policy be adopted that it does not overcome us.
Thus addressed, Arjuna, with joined palms, said to the king, "As you say, so it is, all of it, not otherwise.
But the stroke that is to be dealt to it I shall deal, O Bharata; its destruction lies in the slaying of its chief, and that I shall do."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Then you yourself take Radheya, Bhimasena Suyodhana, Nakula Vrishasena, Sahadeva Subala's son,
Shatanika Duhshasana, the bull of the Shinis Hardikya, Dhrishtadyumna Drona's son, and I myself will go against Kripa.
Let the sons of Draupadi and the rest, with Shikhandin, strike the remaining sons of Dhritarashtra, and let each of mine strike each of our foes."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed by the king of dharma, Dhananjaya said "So be it," ordered his own troops and himself went to the front of the host.
Then, seeing that wondrous chariot approaching, Shalya spoke again to Adhiratha's son, arrogant in battle:

This is the chariot coming, white-horsed with Krishna as charioteer, the son of Kunti slaying enemies, whom you ask about again and again.
mahabharata:8:31.39	A tumultuous noise is heard, the great roar of wheel-rims, and this dust has risen and stands covering the sky.
mahabharata:8:31.40	The earth trembles, Karna, struck by wheel-rims; a great wind blows on all sides of your army; these flesh-eating beasts cry out and make fearful sounds.
mahabharata:8:31.41	See, Karna, a dreadful, fearsome, hair-raising headless trunk like a cloud, standing covering the sun.
mahabharata:8:31.42	See on all sides herds of many kinds of beasts, strong, proud tigers; the sun is seen surrounded.
mahabharata:8:31.43	See herons and vultures in thousands gathered, standing facing us, dreadful, speaking to each other.
mahabharata:8:31.44	Your white horses yoked to your great chariot, Karna—the arrows blaze and the banner trembles.
mahabharata:8:31.45	See the horses rising, huge-bodied, swift, leaping, lovely to behold, like Garudas in the sky.
mahabharata:8:31.46	Surely at these omens, kings will sleep slain around Bhima, Karna, by hundreds and thousands.
mahabharata:8:31.47	The tumultuous, hair-raising sound of conches is heard, of anakas, Radheya, and of mridangas on every side.
mahabharata:8:31.48	Hear, Karna, the many sounds of arrows, the noise of men, horses and chariots, and the sounds of bowstrings and palms of the great.
mahabharata:8:31.49	The banners, made by artisans, of gold and silver with polished garments, of many colours, shine on the chariot, stirred by the wind.
mahabharata:8:31.50	See those pennants of Karna and Arjuna, with gold, moon, stars and sun, with little bells, like lightning in a cloud.
mahabharata:8:31.51	The banners rustle, stirred by the wind, and the chariots with pennants of the great-souled Panchalas.
mahabharata:8:31.52	The banner-tip is seen of him who slays your masses of elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers, and the cry of Victory" is heard.
Today you will see that hero, white-horsed, Krishna as charioteer, slaying foes in battle, of whom you ask, Karna.
Today you will see those two tigers among men, red-eyed scorchers of foes, Vasudeva and Arjuna, Karna, standing on one chariot.
He whose charioteer is the Varshneya and whose bow is Gandiva—if you, Radheya, slay him, you will be our king.
He, challenged by the Samshaptakas, has gone to face them and makes slaughter of those foes in battle, the mighty one." To the king of the Madras speaking thus, Karna, in great anger, replied:
See him, attacked on all sides by the enraged Samshaptakas, covered like the sun by clouds; Partha is not seen. This is the end of Arjuna, Shalya, sunk in the sea of grief.
[Shalya said:] "Who could slay Varuna with water, or fire with fuel? Who could restrain the wind or drink the great ocean?
Such I deem the restraining of Partha in battle; Arjuna cannot be conquered even by all the gods and asuras with Indra.
If you find contentment in saying so, then be glad; he cannot be conquered in battle; set your hopes on something else.
He might lift up the earth with his arms, burn these creatures in anger, or fell the gods from heaven—he who could conquer Arjuna in battle.
See the hero son of Kunti, Bhima of effortless deeds, the mighty-armed, shining, standing like Mount Meru.
Impatient, ever enraged, long remembering enmity, this valiant Bhima stands in battle desiring victory.
This is the best of upholders of dharma, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, who stands in battle hard for enemies to deal with, conqueror of enemy cities.
And these two tigers among men, like the Ashvins brothers, Nakula and Sahadeva, stand in battle hard to conquer.
These sons of Krishna are seen, five like five mountains, standing, all about to fight, equal to Arjuna in battle.
These sons of Drupada led by Dhrishtadyumna, deprived of Satyajit, the heroes stand, of supreme vigour."
As those two lions among men conversed thus, the two armies clashed hard, like the Ganga and Yamuna.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Tell this battle in detail, for you are skilled; I am never satisfied with hearing the heroes' prowess in battle."
[Sanjaya said:] Having placed the great hostile force in position there, Arjuna arrayed his formation against your son's ill-conducted one.
That great army, crowded with horsemen and elephants, thick with infantry and chariots, arrayed by Dhrishtadyumna and the others, shone.
The Parshata, with pigeon-grey and golden horses, as radiant as moon and sun, shone as a bowman, like embodied Time.
The sons of Draupadi, eager to fight, with their followers, of terrible form, stood round the Parshata like stars round the moon.
Then, when the divisions were arrayed, seeing the Samshaptakas in battle, Arjuna, enraged, rushed at them, twanging Gandiva.
Then the Samshaptakas, wishing to kill, ran at Partha, resolved on victory, having made death their return.
That mass of horse, crowded with rutting elephants and chariots, with infantry, with throngs of brave heroes, quickly rushed at Arjuna.
A tumultuous clash took place between them and Kiritin, as we have heard it was with the Nivatakavachas.
Chariots, horses, banners, elephants, foot-soldiers and chariot-lords, arrows, bows, swords, discs and axes,
arms raised with weapons, and weapons raised, Partha cut, and the heads of the foe by thousands.
In that army like a great whirlpool, like the netherworld whirlpool, thinking his chariot submerged, the Samshaptakas roared with joy.
He, killing foes before, behind, on the north and on the south, Bibhatsu enraged was like Rudra among beasts.
Then a most dreadful battle took place, O revered one, between the Panchalas, Chedis and Srinjayas with your men.
Kripa, Kritavarman and Shakuni, Subala's son, with joyful troops, enraged, striking with chariot-divisions,
fought arrogant in battle with the Kosalas, Kashis, Matsyas, Karushas, Kekayas and brave Shurasenas.
Their battle ended lives, destroying the sin of the body, righteous, leading to heaven and bringing fame, of shudra, vaishya and kshatriya heroes.
Duryodhana too, with his brothers, O best of the Bharatas, guarded by Kuru heroes and by the great chariot-warriors of the Madras,
protected Karna, the Kuru hero, fighting in battle against the Pandavas with the Panchalas, the Chedis and Satyaki.
Karna too, slaying the great host with sharp arrows and crushing the best chariot-warriors, tormented Yudhishthira.
Having reduced thousands of foes to lifeless bodies without weapons, and joined with heaven and fame, he brought joy to his own side.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "That which Karna did in entering the Pandava army and making slaughter, and in approaching the king—tell me that, Sanjaya.
Which heroes of the Pandavas held Karna back in battle, and whom did Adhiratha's son crush as he pressed Yudhishthira?"
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing the Pandavas led by Dhrishtadyumna stationed, Karna, tormentor of foes, swiftly ran at the Panchalas.
As he came quickly, the Panchalas, victorious, went to meet him, O great king, like swans to the great ocean.
Then the heart-stirring sound of thousands of conches arose, and on both sides the dreadful roar of kettledrums.
The noise of instruments of many kinds, the sound of elephants, horses and chariots, and the lion-roars of heroes then became fearful.
The earth with its mountains, trees and oceans, the sky with winds and clouds, and the heavens with sun, moon, planets and stars visibly reeled.
Beings felt that sound exceed, and trembled greatly; and the aquatic creatures mostly died.
Then Karna, greatly enraged, uttering swift weapons, slew the Pandava army as Maghavan the asura host.
Entering the Pandava chariots swiftly, loosing arrows, he slew seventy-seven of the foremost Prabhadrakas.
Then with well-feathered sharp arrows, the best of chariot-warriors killed twenty-five Panchalas with twenty-five chariot-arrows.
With golden-feathered iron arrows that tear the bodies of foes, the hero killed the Chedis in hundreds and thousands.
As he performed that superhuman deed in battle, throngs of Panchala chariots surrounded him, O great king.
Then, fixing five irresistible arrows, O Bharata, Karna Vaikartana killed five Panchalas.
Bhanudeva, Chitrasena, Senabindu, Tapana and Shurasena, Panchalas, he killed in battle, O Bharata.
As the brave Panchalas were being slain by arrows, a great cry of "Alas!" arose among the Panchalas in the great battle.
As they were scattered, making the quarters resound with cries of "Alas," Karna killed them swiftly again with feathered arrows.
Karna's two sons, invincible, Sushena and Satyasena, guarding his wheels, fought giving up life, O revered one.
Karna's eldest son, the great chariot-warrior Vrishasena, himself guarded Karna from behind as rear-guard.
Then, in the forenoon, Sanjaya came from the camp and entered the city dejected, filled with sorrow and grief.
The word of the great-souled Vidura has come true; my son did not follow his word, Sanjaya.
Not having followed that counsel, I burn terribly, ill-minded; I did not listen to Bhishma's words, spoken in accord with dharma.
Having caused the slaying of Subhadra's son and the sons of Draupadi, my dear sons, this victory seems to me, Lord, of the nature of defeat.
Let him be thrown in the fire or cut into pieces; this child-killer, this sinner, does not deserve to live long.
Let Karna and Shakuni never see him; be vigilant and prevent even their recourse to gambling.
He also arranged releases from bondage and the release of those condemned; and the king, son of Dharma, never said anything.
This woman, who desires a son, belongs to Babhru of immeasurable splendour; sages, tell well: what will she bear?
This should not be done, they said to the king; but the king, knowing dharma and the turning of time, did not so act.
That which was done through the dice should not be kept in mind, son; you ought not to dwell on the afflictions of Draupadi.
